findings.text: Good: the first line tells a newcomer what Athena is and why it is different (one model does the work, another checks it, costs are recorded). This is all the page says about Athena, though, so nothing shows how Athena works.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This is Athena's home URL, but the title and almost all of the page are about another project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to read the ledes to see that this page is a demo of what Athena can do.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / h1 "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The page does say why it exists, and the bracketed claim ids that link to source lines at a fixed commit make that point convincingly. It never links this study to Athena's main job, turning a request into a code change, so the reader may wonder how the two relate.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: Good: the next step is offered near the top and links to its section, so a newcomer does not have to scroll through the long middle to find it.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: The install steps are thin. There is no clone command, no prerequisites (Rust toolchain, model access or API keys, supported OS), and no word on what `athena ask` produces. A newcomer would have to go to the GitHub repo to actually start.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine with exit codes, lock behaviour and pending-close replays. That suits someone checking firstmate's internals, but it is far more than a first-time visitor needs to judge Athena.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (cards t1–t11), "Claims and sources" (c1–c44)

findings.text: Good: the firstmate summary is plain and comes early. Defining words such as captain, yolo, green and red before they are used helps a newcomer follow the walkthrough.
findings.source: Start here: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker, so that several tasks can run side by side."

findings.text: Some words are used but never defined in the glossary, including endpoint, brief, heartbeat, crewmate, durable record and "main first mate". This weakens the page's promise that it defines the words it uses.
findings.source: t8: "a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead"; c37: "which stays with the main first mate"

findings.text: This refers to a studies/ folder that a newcomer has never seen and cannot reach from the page. It means nothing to a first-time reader without a link to that folder in the repository.
findings.source: About this page: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."

findings.text: Good: the page is open about its limits (nothing was run, and a first reading missed some paths), which helps a newcomer trust it. But f3 names claim ranges like "c26 to c30", which is dense going for a first-time reader.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."
